rationale.rationale: The business being separated is Inox Green's Power Evacuation / substation business — the commissioned substations, 33kV and EHV transmission lines and common evacuation infrastructure sitting on IGESL's balance sheet — which is being demerged out of Inox Green Energy Services Ltd (the wind/solar O&M arm) and merged into Inox Renewable Solutions Ltd (IRSL, formerly Resco Global Wind Services, the group's EPC arm and a subsidiary of parent Inox Wind), with Appointed Date 1 October 2024. Management's core argument is that these assets are not needed to run O&M at all — they exist to deliver turnkey/EPC solutions — so they only inflate IGESL's balance sheet and depress its returns: Inox Green was described as merely the 'trustee' of substations customers had already paid for, and the asset block was explained as a legacy of IGESL having once housed both the EPC and O&M businesses, where the pre-IPO slump sale of EPC to Resco could not carry over already-commissioned infra because that would have required consent from over 200 customers who would have reopened O&M contracts — hence the NCLT scheme route. The quantified benefit moved from a net block of ~INR750 crore (Aug 2024) to a gross block of ~INR1,000 crore leaving the books, with annual depreciation of ~INR50–55 crore eliminated (quarterly depreciation had been running INR13–17 crore, i.e. ~INR12 crore added to quarterly PAT), against only a token revenue loss — first put at INR4–5 crore a year, then INR3–4 crore a quarter, and finally ~INR10 crore. With no depreciation, virtually nil finance cost and ~INR700 crore of carried-forward tax losses that stay at company level (losses attach to the company, not the asset), management says EBITDA converts to PBT, PAT and cash profit, so the ~INR600 crore FY27 EBITDA guidance is effectively all operating cash, and ROE/ROCE improve 'significantly'. The scheme's own rationale adds that O&M and Power Evacuation have separate and distinct risk, reward, financial profile, competition and opportunity sets, that evacuation infra can attract a different investor/partner/lender base, that consolidating the same line of business into IRSL unlocks value and focus, and that the outcome is two listed entities — a pure-play O&M company and an EPC/evacuation company — each free to pursue its own strategy. Consideration is paid in IRSL shares to IGESL shareholders (122 IRSL shares per 1,000 IGESL shares; management earlier framed it as IGESL shareholders owning ~20% of Resco, 10% minority and 10% promoters), with IRSL automatically listing — which management (Devansh Jain, Sanjeev Agarwal) says 'unlocks substantial value' for both Inox Wind and Inox Green and gives a shareholder the choice of holding the O&M business, the infrastructure business, or the whole value chain via Inox Wind. No lender or counterparty demand was cited; secured creditors, unsecured creditors, warrant and debenture holders and shareholders all approved the scheme unanimously or with requisite majority, and analysts/retail holders (Hansal Thakkar on rationalising subsidiaries, Pradyumna Choudhary and Pradeep Motwani on timelines and value unlocking for minority shareholders) pushed management on it rather than originating it.
rationale.evolution: The idea first surfaced as a board action on the 9 Aug 2024 call (Q1 FY25), where consultants and registered valuers had been appointed to evaluate demerging the power evacuation business for a 'cleaner and asset light balance sheet', and Devansh Jain explained on that same call why the infra could not be moved at the pre-IPO EPC slump sale (200+ customer consents); by the 25 Oct 2024 call (tagged Nov 2024) valuation was underway with a quantified ~INR12 crore quarterly PAT uplift and IGESL shareholders to receive Resco shares, and the board approved the scheme on 13 Nov 2024 with Appointed Date 1 Oct 2024. On 31 Jan 2025 (Feb 2025 tag) Akhil Jindal promised an 'asset-light balance sheet' with no depreciation 'next year', ~20% of Resco to IGESL shareholders and confirmation that the ~INR700 crore tax losses stay with IGESL; by 1 Sep 2025 exchange no-objections were in and the scheme was filed at NCLT Ahmedabad with the figure firmed up at ~INR1,000 crore gross block and INR50–55 crore depreciation plus ROE/ROCE gains, and on 14 Nov 2025 shareholder and creditor approvals were announced. The 13 Feb 2026 call put it in 'final stages of hearing' with only ~INR10 crore of revenue leaving, and the 29 May 2026 call confirmed NCLT approval (order 13 Mar 2026); filings then show the scheme effective 4 May 2026, record date 1 Aug 2026 and 4,89,82,030 IRSL shares allotted on 24 Aug 2026 — with the only real change in plan being management's Sep 2025 rejection of any further demerger of IGESL/IRSL out of Inox Wind itself.

points.point: Early framing of IGESL as an asset-light annuity business with all future common-infrastructure capex deliberately routed to Resco, not Inox Green — the precursor logic to removing the legacy block.
points.quote: And any future CapEx which we intend to incur in developing our common infra will be done in Resco and not under Inox Green.

points.point: The board formally started the process by appointing consultants and registered valuers, with the stated purpose of a cleaner, asset-light balance sheet and depreciation elimination.
points.quote: Demerger of power infrastructure facilities currently on the balance sheet of Inox Green will result in a cleaner and asset light balance sheet.

points.point: Devansh Jain gave the historical reason the assets were stranded at IGESL: moving commissioned substations at the pre-IPO EPC slump sale would have needed consent from over 200 customers who would have renegotiated O&M contracts.
points.quote: We could not shunt it out from this balance sheet into Resco because that would have entailed taking approval from over 200 customers and then arm twisting us in terms of renegotiating contracts and screwing the entire O&M business.

points.point: He characterised IGESL as only the trustee of substations customers had already paid for, so the balance sheet was inflated for no economic reason; net block then put at ~INR750 crore and the model described as zero-capex annuity.
points.quote: Inox Green's balance sheet is unnecessarily inflated thanks to these historical substations which are lying on its balance sheet of which we are actually the trustee.

points.point: First quantification of the trade-off: only ~INR3–4 crore of quarterly revenue exits while the entire depreciation goes, adding ~INR12 crore to quarterly PAT; consideration to IGESL holders is Resco shares.
points.quote: Excluding the substation business , the revenue would be down by around Rs. 3 crores or Rs. 4 crores on a quarterly basis , and the whole depreciation will go away. So, broadly that will add around Rs. 12-odd crore in the bottom line on a quarterly basis.

points.point: Akhil Jindal set the end-state: an asset-light balance sheet with no depreciation as a continuing item, so EBITDA becomes the benchmark for PAT; Mathusudhana added IGESL shareholders would own ~20% of Resco (10% minority, 10% promoters).
points.quote: So when you're looking into the next year's balance sheet of Inox Green, it would be an asset - light balance sheet. And it would also have no depreciation charges as a continued item.

points.point: Confirmed the ~INR700 crore of accumulated tax losses are not stripped out with the assets, because losses sit at company level — key to EBITDA converting to cash PAT.
points.quote: So the tax losses would be on a company level, not on an asset level. So the tax losses will remain in this company.

points.point: Answering whether depreciation simply becomes opex, management argued the evacuation and common infrastructure is irrelevant to O&M delivery and belongs with the turnkey/EPC business.
points.quote: So as far as the power evacuation and the common infrastructure, we have developed is not required for O&M services per se. That is required for further providing a turnkey solution to the customers.

points.point: With exchange no-objections received and the scheme filed at NCLT Ahmedabad, the benefit was firmed up at ~INR1,000 crore gross block off the books, INR50–55 crore of annual depreciation eliminated and higher ROE/ROCE.
points.quote: Once the scheme is approved by the NCLT, the gross block of around INR1,000 crore will be off our balance sheet and subsequently the depreciation of approximately INR50 crores to INR55 crores annually will be eliminated , thereby increasing the PBT by that amount.

points.point: Asked by a shareholder whether IGESL and IRSL would be demerged out of Inox Wind to IWL holders, management refused — the only separation intended was the infra assets into Resco, which then lists, giving holders a choice of exposure.
points.quote: And I think from a shareholder's perspective, a shareholder has got now a choice to hold any part of the business. He can hold the O&M business, he can hold the infrastructure business, he can hold the entire value chain together under Inox Wind.

points.point: Shareholder and creditor approvals obtained; the benefit framed as two-sided — IRSL listing as Inox Wind's EPC arm, and depreciation elimination at Inox Green.
points.quote: This will add value for both Inox Wind, with subsequent listing of Inox Renewable solution as an EPC arm of Inox Wind, and Inox Green with elimination of depreciation on demergers of the asset blocks

points.point: Devansh Jain put the value-unlocking claim explicitly on the demerger plus subsequent listing of IRSL.
points.quote: I believe that the de -merger and subsequent listing of Inox Renewable Solutions will unlock substantial value for both Inox Wind and Inox Green.

points.point: In the final NCLT hearing stage, management reiterated the asymmetry — about INR10 crore of revenue leaves versus ~INR50 crore of depreciation — i.e. no material revenue impact.
points.quote: So post the demerger, as we have clarified on the multiple cores, there would be a very limited amount of revenue in the range of INR 10 odd crore will get out of the balance sheet. And around INR 50 odd crore s of depreciation will go out from the balance sheet.

points.point: Post NCLT approval, Mathusudhana confirmed the ~INR1,000 crore gross block and INR50–55 crore annual depreciation had been eliminated, with ROE and ROCE significantly improved; IRSL to be automatically listed.
points.quote: With this gross block of approximately INR1,000 crores has been eliminated from Inox Green's balance sheet. And subsequently, the annual depreciation of approximately INR50 crores to INR55 crores has been eliminated, thereby increasing the profitability.

points.point: The cash-conversion payoff: with no depreciation, no finance cost and a ~INR700 crore tax shield, the FY27 INR600 crore EBITDA guidance is treated as essentially all operating cash flow for Inox Green shareholders.
points.quote: As such, there will be no depreciation, no finance cost, and we have a tax shield up to INR700 crore of losses.

points.point: Devansh Jain placed the IRSL demerger in a sequence of value-creation corporate actions after spinning off Inox Green, while deflecting criticism of the share price.
points.quote: We're on the verge of demerging Inox Renewable Solutions, which we hope will create tremendous value.

points.point: The scheme's rationale rests on segregating verticals with different economics, since risk, reward, financial profile, competition and opportunity differ between O&M and Power Evacuation.
points.quote: The nature of rislcs, rewards, financial profile, competition and opportunities are separate and distinct for the O&M services business and the Power Evacuation Business.

points.point: A second stated reason is a different capital-provider base for the evacuation business, plus consolidation of the same line of business into IRSL to unlock value and sharpen focus, leaving IGESL a pure-play O&M player.
points.quote: Further, the Power Evacuation Business is capable of attracting different set of investors, strategic partners, lenders and other stakeholders.

points.point: Consideration mechanics: IGESL shareholders receive IRSL shares in a 122:1,000 ratio (valuation by Finvox Analytics, fairness opinion by Marwadi Chandarana), Appointed Date 1 Oct 2024, scheme effective 4 May 2026, 4,89,82,030 IRSL shares allotted 24 Aug 2026.
points.quote: 122 equity shares of IRSL (face value Rs. 10/- each) shall be issued for every 1,000 equity shares (face value Rs. 10/- each) held in Inox Green Energy Services Limited.

IRSL: consolidated EPC/evacuation platform, separately listed, its own investors and lenders, value unlocked for Inox Wind and Inox Green holders.

judge.selling_pressure_why: Entitlement is only 1 PFEL share per 9 PAIL shares; sugar is a different, seasonal industry premium-spirits holders did not buy.

rationale.rationale: Management is demerging the Sugar Business of Piccadily Agro Industries Ltd. (PAIL) into Piccadily Food & Essentials Limited (PFEL), a wholly owned subsidiary, so that PAIL becomes a pure-play premium alco-bev company; CFO Natwar Aggarwal framed it on the April 29, 2026 call as "we want to be a global alco-bev company and in that pursuit we want to focus on our core brand portfolio," with the scheme Board-approved April 28, 2026, filed with SEBI, KPMG as adviser, and completion envisaged in FY27. The stated intent is to pool human and capital resources behind the Alco-Bev portfolio (Indri single malt, Camikara rum, Cashmir vodka, Whistler blended whisky) and to list sugar — described as a "traditional heritage business" — as a separate entity rather than sell it. The economics behind it are visible in the numbers management cited: Alco-Bev revenue grew 42% to INR 908 crore (from INR 639 crore) with 31.5% EBITDA margins and 45–50% IMFL margins, while sugar was only INR 233.05 crore of turnover (20.53% of the listed entity) and dragged Q4 standalone EBITDA margin down ~300 bps as sugar's quarterly EBITDA margin collapsed from 11% to 2%; the segment tables show the sugar segment result at a loss of INR 904.62 lakh in FY26 versus a loss of INR 327.13 lakh in FY25, with sugar segment assets of INR 10,553.97 lakh against segment liabilities of INR 22,166.79 lakh. Management also repeatedly blamed sugar seasonality for making quarter-to-quarter margins hard to read. The scheme's own rationale (Annexure B) lists focused attention for each core business and the ability to attract required investment, greater business focus and enhanced shareholder value, more efficient use of financial resources, managerial talent, technical skills and marketing resources, value unlock "through price-discovery of the individual entities," the "right operating architecture" with sharper individual strategies and "clear capital allocation," and separately listed companies attracting a specific set of investors with financial flexibility and "stronger capital market outcomes." Mechanically it is a mirror listing: no cash consideration, 1 PFEL share of INR 10 for every 9 PAIL shares (ratio fixed on sugar's turnover and assets), PFEL's pre-scheme capital cancelled, no change in PAIL's shareholding pattern, producing "two listed companies with proportionate shareholding." No investor, lender or business partner is identified anywhere as having demanded the separation — it is presented as a management/Board decision, recommended by the Audit Committee and Independent Directors, alongside the unrelated FY27 agenda of INR 250–300 crore incremental Indri revenue, INR 300–400 crore from the 200 KLPD Chhattisgarh plant, 60–70% growth and brand-side inorganic options.
rationale.evolution: Only one earnings call falls in the window, the FY26 call of April 29, 2026, and the demerger appears there already as a done decision rather than an idea being floated — announced in the CFO's opening remarks the day after the April 28, 2026 Board meeting approved the scheme and filed it with the exchanges/SEBI, with KPMG as partner and FY27 as the completion target. It resurfaced later in the same call only when Himanshu Shah of Dolat Capital pressed on intent (sell or separately list), drawing the explicit answer that sugar would be listed separately, not sold. The filings then track execution rather than rationale: the April 28, 2026 Regulation 30 outcome with the full Annexure B rationale, share entitlement ratio and sugar turnover of INR 233.05 crore (20.53%), the April 28, 2026 press release restating the pure-play framing, and the August 17, 2026 intimation of BSE/NSE no-adverse-observation letters dated August 14, 2026 (SEBI comments dated August 13, 2026) clearing the way for the NCLT petition. Earlier filings in the window (November–December 2025) concern only CCD and warrant conversions and never mention a separation.

rationale.rationale: Management presented this as a two-part move announced on 20 March 2026: TCIL demerges its own Resorts and Resort Management undertaking — the six resorts it owns/operates directly under the Nature Trails brand (adventure holidays, educational trips, corporate getaways), with turnover of only INR 70 crore for the year ended 31 December 2025, about 0.4% of TCIL's standalone turnover — into Sterling Holiday Resorts Limited (SHRL), its wholly owned hospitality subsidiary, which is then listed on BSE and NSE. The boards' first reason is capability fit: the resort business 'would reap more benefit from being owned and operated by SHRL in light of their vast expertise in the hospitality industry' (SHRL had 72+ resorts across 62 locations at announcement, 78 resorts/~3,800 rooms/65 destinations by FY26). The second is that SHRL has 'matured' and is 'well poised to chart its own growth path' as a separate listed entity — FY26 revenue INR 5,487mn, EBITDA INR 1,701mn (31% margin), PBT INR 1,142mn (21%), 25 consecutive profitable quarters, ~INR 3,400mn cash at a 55% multi-year CAGR, debt-free, targeting 95 resorts and 4,500 rooms in 2027. The third is investor-facing: unlock value, 'attract differentiated investor cohorts for each business segment', and let two listed entities pursue growth aligned to their own industry dynamics with improved operational efficiency and profitability, while TCIL concentrates on core Travel and Financial Services (FY26 group income INR 83,982mn, EBT INR 3,268mn, down 14% on the Pahalgam/Operation Sindoor and US-Israel-Iran disruptions). Riding along are three capital-structure fixes: consolidation of four Re.1 shares into one Rs.4 share to improve key financial ratios and better reflect intrinsic value; a reduction of face value from Rs.4 to Rs.3 with no payout to 'right size the balance sheet' and improve EPS; and absorption of three dormant subsidiaries (TC Visa Services, Jardin Travel Solutions, Borderless Travel Services) that incur 'unnecessary compliance and administrative costs'. Consideration is non-cash: 81 SHRL shares of Rs.10 for every 100 TCIL shares of Re.1; TCIL keeps its existing SHRL shares (~7%); SHRL's post-scheme pattern mirrors TCIL's (promoters 65.55%, public 32.30%, ESOP trust 2.16%). The documented originators are internal — the Audit Committee and the Independent Directors Committee recommended it to the Board; no investor, lender, franchise or JV partner is cited anywhere as having asked for it, and the capital-deployment questions analysts did press (Mukul Varma, Anil Shah, Meet Shah on the ~INR 780-800 crore net cash and dividends) were answered with 'no conversations' as late as February 2026.
rationale.evolution: Nothing in the Q4 FY25 call (14 May 2025) or Q1 FY26 call (1 August 2025) hints at a separation, though both lay the groundwork: TCIL had just absorbed the Nature Trails resorts business by slump sale in March 2025 for INR 522.5mn, and Vikram Lalvani declared Sterling's 'transformation is complete' and in a growth phase, debt-free with rising cash. The Q2 FY26 (14 November 2025) and Q3 FY26 (6 February 2026) calls still carry no mention — on 6 February 2026 Mahesh Iyer explicitly said there were no conversations on returning cash or acquisitions, six weeks before the Board acted. The Board gave in-principle approval on 20 March 2026 (Scheme, press release, and separate demerger/merger/consolidation/capital-reduction filings), and the first and only call discussion came on 13 May 2026, where Iyer called it a 'strategic divestment… significant strategic move', Lalvani confirmed 'the demerger process from Thomas Cook has also been initiated', and Debasis Nandy reaffirmed the original 12-15 month timeline with completion expected in Q1 FY28. Execution then ran ahead of the calls: BSE no-adverse-observation (31 August 2026), NSE no-objection (1 September 2026), and an NCLT Mumbai procedural order of 4 November 2026 admitting the application and directing meetings of TCIL's equity shareholders and unsecured creditors.

points.point: Regulatory progress since: BSE no-adverse-observation (31 Aug 2026), NSE no-objection (1 Sep 2026), and an NCLT Mumbai order of 4 November 2026 admitting the application and directing TCIL shareholder and unsecured-creditor meetings.

rationale.rationale: No earnings-call transcripts are on file, so the reasoning below is reconstructed only from the filings. The separation is the demerger of Valor Estate Ltd's (formerly D B Realty Ltd) hospitality business into Advent Hotels International Limited (formerly Shiva Realtors Suburban Private Limited) under a Composite Scheme of Amalgamation and Arrangement that also amalgamated Esteem Properties Private Limited into Valor; the Explanatory Statement to the 12th December 2025 EGM says the Scheme was entered into 'mainly with aim to demerge hospitality business of the Company into Resulting Company and thus unlock overall value for the shareholders.' NCLT Mumbai sanctioned it on 12 June 2025, it became effective 1 July 2025 (demerger appointed date 1 April 2025; Esteem amalgamation appointed date 1 April 2024), and shareholders on the 18 July 2025 record date received 1 AHIL share of Rs. 10 for every 10 Valor shares. The carve-out moved consolidated net assets of Rs. 1,02,194.65 lakhs (standalone Rs. 1,01,512.91 lakhs) out of Valor — Rs. 1,49,386.00 lakhs of property, plant and equipment, Rs. 54,858.00 lakhs of goodwill, Rs. 29,117.12 lakhs of intangibles, against Rs. 46,196.17 lakhs non-current and Rs. 16,028.03 lakhs current borrowings, Rs. 2,01,956.25 lakhs of other non-current financial liabilities and Rs. 28,951.71 lakhs of deferred tax liability — and took out a business that had FY25 revenue of Rs. 36,650.21 lakhs and PAT of Rs. 4,468.06 lakhs, now shown as discontinued operations. Management's stated problems solved are focus and structure: Valor 'is now engaged solely in the real estate business, which constitutes its only reportable segment,' so segment reporting ceased, while Advent gets 'its own Board and Management team,' NSE/BSE listing on 13 November 2025 for 'enhanced market visibility, liquidity for existing shareholders, and a strengthened capital structure,' and an asset-heavy growth path (five projects, 3,100 keys, EBITDA from under Rs. 200 crore to over Rs. 1,200 crore by FY32, targeted mid-teens compounded ROE) that a combined entity would have had to fund alongside real estate. The second, smaller separation/consolidation strand is non-core cleanup: Sahyadri Agro and Dairy Private Limited (dairy farming, milk procurement and trading), taken to 76.63% via enforcement of security and then to 100% 'as the transaction relates to the liquidation of non-core assets,' sold its entire dairy business under a Business Transfer Agreement at a gain of Rs. 6,901.20 lakhs with Rs. 1,697.63 lakhs of non-compete fees booked as an exceptional item, is now 'evaluating opportunities to engage in the business of real estate development,' and was amalgamated into Horizontal Ventures Private Limited for structural simplification, synergies, avoidance of duplication and lower compliance and overhead costs. Running alongside is balance-sheet repair the filings tie to the same strategy: consolidated secured debt down to Rs. 730 crore, full redemption of Rs. 235 crore of NCDs out of the Rs. 262 crore Dahisar/Aradhya Park development-rights conveyance, and the Scheme-driven reduction and consolidation of the 8% RPS (Clause 32: Rs. 10 face value cut to Rs. 9, then 10 consolidated into 9) plus Clause 20's 1:10 allotment of AHIL preference shares, followed by the November 2025 proposal to convert KRPL's 6,45,75,000 RPS into 0.0001% CCPS converting into 32,02,330 equity shares at Rs. 201.65 'with a view to conserve the financial resources of the Company.' No filing names any investor, lender or partner as having demanded the separation; the only named partner is Prestige Group, which sits on Advent's side as a 50:50 JV partner in the Sahar project and co-developer at Aerocity.
rationale.evolution: There are no transcripts on file, so the idea cannot be traced call by call; the paper trail runs through filings and the Scheme itself. The Composite Scheme was sanctioned by NCLT Mumbai on 12 June 2025, became effective 1 July 2025 with demerger appointed date 1 April 2025, and the 1:10 entitlement was fixed on the 18 July 2025 record date; the SADPL-into-HVPL amalgamation was approved by both boards on 18 August 2025 with appointed date 1 April 2025. The plan then became visible in public filings in quick succession: Advent's listing press release (12 November 2025), Valor's Q2FY26 results and press release (14-15 November 2025) which first framed the demerger as completed and as the basis for debt reduction, the EGM notice and corrigendum (20 November and 8 December 2025) which disclosed the Scheme's preference-share reduction, consolidation and 1:10 AHIL allotment and layered the RPS-to-CCPS conversion on top, and finally the NCLT order of 29 January 2026 and effective date of 12 March 2026 completing the SADPL consolidation. The shape of the plan therefore widened over time from a single hospitality demerger into a package: demerger plus listing, plus non-core dairy liquidation and merger, plus capital-structure conversion.

points.point: The Composite Scheme's stated purpose, as put to shareholders in the EGM explanatory statement, was to demerge the hospitality business into Advent Hotels International Limited and unlock shareholder value; it simultaneously amalgamated Esteem Properties Private Limited into Valor.

points.point: Building on the Scheme, the Board on 14 November 2025 proposed converting KRPL's 6,45,75,000 8% RPS into 0.0001% CCPS convertible into 32,02,330 equity shares at Rs. 201.65 (premium Rs. 191.65), to avoid the redemption cash outflow and lift net worth.

rationale.what_management_expects: Valor: pure-play real estate, single reportable segment, leaner and more efficient capital structure, lower debt (secured debt ₹730 crore), greater financial flexibility, unlocked value. Advent: independent board and management, focused hospitality platform, better visibility, shareholder liquidity, stronger capital structure, 3,100 keys and EBITDA above ₹1,200 crore by FY32, mid-teens compounded ROE.

rationale.rationale: HEGAM's separation is the "Composite Scheme of Arrangement" among HEG Advanced Materials Limited (formerly HEG Limited, the Demerged Company), HEG Limited (formerly HEG Graphite Limited, the Resulting Company) and Bhilwara Energy Limited (the Transferor Company): the legacy Graphite Undertaking — the graphite electrodes business, plus the overseas investment and the assets and liabilities of the TAWA power plant — was demerged into the Resulting Company on a going-concern basis with mirror shares issued to HEGAM shareholders, while Bhilwara Energy Limited was simultaneously amalgamated into HEGAM. As the filings present it, the purpose is to put the mature, cyclical electrodes business (FY26 revenue ₹2,568.50 crore, H1 FY27 ₹1,207.36 crore and PAT ₹192.33 crore, carrying ₹4,419.21 crore of segment assets and ₹1,245.85 crore of liabilities) in one listed vehicle, and leave HEGAM as a "technology-led, globally competitive advanced materials platform" spanning anode materials (TACC), graphene (HEG Graphene Materials), battery energy storage (Replus Engitech, 74% held) and green power. The amalgamation of Bhilwara Energy brings 278 MW of debt-free hydro (86 MW MPCL + 192 MW AD Hydro) plus 14 MW of wind into HEGAM, which the CFO says "provides a sound financial foundation for the Group" with "stable cash flows of over ₹300 crore" annually — i.e. the hydro cash flow and the ₹1,322.84 crore cash pile now sit against the heavy new-materials capex rather than against electrodes. The problem it solves is capital allocation and identity: HEGAM's board on 3 November 2026 approved a revised Phase-1 anode cost of ~₹2,350 crore (20,000 MT, COD June 2027, 61% built), a ₹1,606 crore Phase-2 to 44,000 MT by March 2029, a ₹475 crore crucible plant for "backward integration" and cost optimisation, and a ₹500 crore 500 MTPA graphene plant — none of which belong on an electrode balance sheet. The company also altered its main object clause to insert "Anode, Graphene, crucible, advanced carbon materials and other allied material" (CIN changed from L23109MP1972PLC008290 to L35100MP1972PLC008290) and implemented an ESOP of up to 98,93,970 options, so each entity can be objected, incentivised and financed on its own. Leadership was split along the same line: Ravi Jhunjhunwala moved to Chairman, MD & CEO of the demerged HEG Limited (graphite), while Riju Jhunjhunwala leads HEGAM and has now taken the chair of MPCL and AD Hydro. A lender appears in the record on the power side: CYHPL bought Statkraft's 49% of MPCL on 17 November 2025 and intends to merge MPCL and ADHPL into itself "for consolidating the hydro power asstes of the group in the CYHPL in line with undertaking given by CYHPL to ICICI Bank."
rationale.evolution: No earnings-call transcripts were supplied, so the sequence can only be traced through filings: by 19 January 2026 the Scheme was already public enough to warrant an investor "Webinar on Update on Composite Scheme of Arrangement," and the 49% MPCL buy-out from Statkraft (SPA 9 September 2025, closed 17 November 2025) had pre-positioned the hydro assets. Shareholders approved it at the NCLT-convened meeting on 5 May 2026 with requisite majority; the NCLT Indore Bench sanctioned it on 13 August 2026; the board fixed 1 September 2026 as Effective Date (Appointed Date backdated to 1 April 2024) and allotted the new shares on 7 September 2026, lifting paid-up capital from ₹38.60 crore to ₹65.96 crore. Only after effectiveness did the plan visibly widen from "separate graphite" to "build out advanced materials": the 3 November 2026 board added Phase-2 anode (44,000 MT), crucibles, graphene, an ESOP and the new object clause, while on 29–30 October 2026 the object-clause CIN change was registered and HEGAM had to publish the unlisted Resulting Company's results on its behalf pending listing.

points.point: The Scheme's core mechanic: the Graphite Undertaking — including the overseas investment and the TAWA power plant assets and liabilities — goes out to the Resulting Company, and Bhilwara Energy comes in.
points.quote: the demerger of the Graphite Undertaking including overseas investment and assets and liabilities pertaining to TAWA power plant of the Company into the Resulting Company and amalgamation of the Transferor Company with the Company

points.point: The press release states plainly what moved where on the 1 September 2026 effective date, and that the two sides are now reported separately as continuing and discontinued operations.
points.quote: Under the Scheme, the graphite electrodes business was transferred to HEG Limited (earlier known as HEG Graphite Limited), and Bhilwara Energy Limited was amalgamated into the Company.

points.point: Riju Jhunjhunwala frames the remaining entity's purpose as a technology-led advanced materials platform across anode, graphene, BESS and green power, with "research to revenue" as the motto.
points.quote: Q2 FY27 reflects our continued progress towards building HEG Advanced Materials into a technology -led, globally competitive advanced materials platform.

points.point: CFO Neha Rajvanshi explains the financial logic of pulling hydro in: the debt-free green power business funds and underwrites the developmental verticals.
points.quote: Our Green Power Business, with its differentiated model, profitable operations, debt -free position and stable cash flows, provides a sound financial foundation for the Group.

points.point: The scale of that foundation: 278 MW of hydro in Himachal (86 MW MPCL + 192 MW AD Hydro) plus 14 MW wind, all debt-free, against H1 FY27 cash of ₹1,322.84 crore.
points.quote: Both operating hydro projects and the wind project are debt -free, and the existing hydro assets generate annually stable cash flows of over ₹300 crore.

points.point: Immediately post-demerger the board sanctioned the capex the new entity exists to carry: Phase-1 20,000 MT anode revised to ~₹2,350 crore (COD June 2027), Phase-2 24,000 MT for ~₹1,606 crore to reach 44,000 MT by March 2029.
points.quote: Proposal for expansion plan by increasing the capacity from 20,000 MT to 44,000 MT.  The estimated cost is ~ Rs. 1606 crore with target COD by March 2029.

points.point: The ₹475 crore, 80,000-unit crucible plant is justified as backward integration into the anode line rather than as a new market.
points.quote: The project is expected to strengthen backward integration, optimize procurement costs, and improve operational  efficiencies,  thereby supporting the long-term growth and competitiveness of the subsidiary.

points.point: The ₹500 crore, 500 MTPA graphene plant in HEG Graphene Materials Limited is positioned as a new growth avenue built through a subsidiary.
points.quote: The proposed project is expected to create a new avenue for business growth through the subsidiary, strengthen the Company's long-term business prospects, and contribute to sustainable  value  creation  for stakeholders

points.point: The legal identity was re-pointed at the new businesses: the object clause was amended to insert anode, graphene, crucible and advanced carbon materials, which changed the CIN from L23109MP1972PLC008290 to L35100MP1972PLC008290.
points.quote: Alteration of the main object clause of Memorandum of Association (MOA) of the company by inserting the objects relating to Anode, Graphene, crucible, advanced carbon materials and other allied material, subject to the approval of shareholders.

points.point: A lender's requirement drives the parallel power-side restructuring: CYHPL, having bought Statkraft's 49% of MPCL on 17 November 2025, plans to acquire the remaining 51% and merge MPCL and ADHPL into itself.
points.quote: Theproposed acquisition andmerger isbeing done forconsolidating thehydro power asstes of the group in the CYHPL in line with undertaking given by CYHPL to ICICI Bank.

points.point: Shareholders, not just the board, carried the Scheme — approved at the NCLT-convened meeting of 5 May 2026, sanctioned by NCLT Indore on 13 August 2026, effective 1 September 2026 with 1 April 2024 as appointed date.
points.quote: The equity shareholders at the NCLT -convened meeting held on May 05, 2026  have passed the resolution with requisite majority approv ing the Scheme .

points.point: Management had been briefing investors on the Scheme well before effectiveness, via a dedicated webinar in January 2026.
points.quote: Please find below the link for Video Recording of Webinar on Update on Composite Scheme of Arrangement held on 19th January, 2026 at 1600 hrs IST.

points.point: The split is also a leadership and generational split: Ravi Jhunjhunwala took the graphite entity, Riju Jhunjhunwala runs HEGAM and from 3 November 2026 chairs MPCL and AD Hydro.
points.quote: He was the Chairman, Managing Director & CEO of HEG Limited (now renamed as HEG Advanced Materials Limited ), (until effectiveness of the Composite Scheme of Arrangement) .

points.point: Reporting consequence management flags for investors: the two halves are no longer comparable, and the unlisted Resulting Company's results are being published through HEGAM until its shares list.
points.quote: Current financial figures are not comparable to previous financial figures owing to demerger of HEG Limited.

rationale.what_management_expects: Graphite stands alone as HEG Limited (FY26 revenue ₹2,568.50 crore), pending listing. HEGAM becomes a focused advanced-materials platform — anode 20,000→44,000 MT, crucibles, 500 MTPA graphene, Replus BESS (1→6 GWh), 278 MW debt-free hydro giving ₹300 crore-plus annual cash flow and ₹1,322.84 crore cash to fund capex — with diversified revenues, ESOP-aligned talent and "multiple avenues for value creation."

rationale.rationale: This is not a sale but a three-way split by demerger: a Scheme of Arrangement approved by MSL's board (first on 22 May 2026, then re-approved 7 October 2026 with an Appointed Date of 1 October 2026) carves two 'Demerged Undertakings' out of Maharashtra Seamless into two wholly owned subsidiaries that will themselves be listed on BSE and NSE. Demerged Undertaking 1 — the Mangaon, Maharashtra seamless pipe plant (125,000 MTPA) plus the 10 MW captive solar plant at Beed — goes to MSL Seamless Tubes Limited (MSTL); Demerged Undertaking 2 — the Narketpally, Telangana seamless mill (200,000 MTPA), the Khetusar (20 MW) and Pokhran (5 MW) solar plants in Rajasthan, and the rig Jindal Explorer — goes to United Seamless Limited (USL), i.e. the asset base MSL bought out of IBC as United Seamless Tubulaar for INR477 crores plus INR73 crores of reactivation capex. On FY2025-26 operational turnover the split is Undertaking 1 INR793 crores (16.98%), Undertaking 2 INR693 crores (14.84%) and the residual company (Nagothane pipes, ERW, treasury) INR3,185 crores (68.18%) of INR4,671 crores. The board's stated reasons are that the undertakings have 'distinct geographies, product profiles, technologies used, operational requirements, customer profile and base, market focus, logistics consideration' — specifically three different mill technologies, CPE at Nagothane, MPM at Mangaon and FQM at Telangana, each needing its own modernization and technical expertise — so each should run as a focused, independently reported vertical. It also says manufacturing, drilling and renewable energy have 'different capital intensity and funding requirements', so splitting them allows better assessment of capital needs and more flexibility for expansion; the renewable plants are attached to the mills they can power; and the rig business, long described on calls as outside the core, is segregated because it has 'distinct operational and commercial characteristics as compared to the pipe manufacturing business'. No cash changes hands: shareholders get 1 share of INR5 in each resulting company for every 5 MSL shares, producing the same proportionate holding (promoter ~70.30%, public ~29.70%, 2,67,99,850 shares in each), which the filing calls 'value neutral'; creditor liabilities are neither reduced nor extinguished and travel with each undertaking. Notably, the nine earnings calls supplied — including Feb 2026, three months before the first board approval — contain no mention of a demerger at all; the only antecedents are repeated investor pressure to exit the rig and one shareholder's demand to split the company, and management's standing answer that it would continue 'in the steel pipe segment only' and that exit was 'for the Board to decide'.
rationale.evolution: The idea surfaced only as a rig exit: on the Feb 2024 call (30 Jan 2024) Chairman D.P. Jindal said of staying in rigs 'we have to take the appropriate decision at the right time', and on the Nov 2024 call (29 Oct 2024) an investor asked directly about demerging or selling the rig, to which management said it was something 'we want to do, but it is subject to Board approval'. Pressure widened over the next year: on the Feb 2025 call (28 Jan 2025) management personally agreed the rig-to-Jindal-Drilling structure 'doesn't look in line' with its governance clean-up, on the Jun 2025 call (27 May 2025) it confirmed 'there was a view of getting out of the rig business' with no board update, and on the Aug 2025 call (31 July 2025) a shareholder explicitly asked management to 'divide the company in two parts' — a holding company and a seamless company — and got only 'I don't have anything to add'. By the Nov 2025 call (5 Nov 2025) there was still 'no update on the proposal', and the Feb 2026 call (29 Jan 2026) discussed only cash conservation, treasury and a hunt for distressed acquisitions. The actual plan then appeared without any call commentary: board approval 22 May 2026, a 15 June 2026 notice that the Scheme was 'under further review', and a revised, re-approved Scheme on 7 October 2026 that widened it from a rig/holding split into a full three-way break-up of the three mills by technology, with 'related assets and liabilities' tightened to 'specified assets and liabilities' and 'mirror shareholding' restated as 'same proportionate shareholding'.

points.point: Two undertakings are carved out into two wholly owned subsidiaries, MSL Seamless Tubes Limited and United Seamless Limited, both to be listed, with an Appointed Date of 1 October 2026; the Mangaon 125,000 MTPA mill and the 10 MW Beed captive solar plant form Undertaking 1.
points.quote: Demerged Undertaking 1: Seamless pipe manufacturing business of the Demerged Company located at Mangaon, Maharashtra (125,000 MTPA), captive solar power plant at Beed, Maharashtra (10 MW), along with the specified assets and liabilities of Demerged Undertaking 1.

points.point: Undertaking 2 bundles the Telangana (Narketpally) 200,000 MTPA mill with the Rajasthan solar plants and the rig Jindal Explorer into United Seamless Limited — effectively re-separating the ex-United Seamless Tubulaar asset base and the rig in one entity.
points.quote: Demerged Undertaking 2: Seamless pipe manufacturing facility of the Demerged Company located at Narketpally, Telangana (200,000 MTPA), solar power plants at Khetusar (20 MW) & Pokhran (5MW) in Rajasthan, rig Jindal Explorer along with the specified assets and liabilities of Demerged Undertaking 2.

points.point: The headline justification is that one company holds businesses with nothing in common operationally — different geographies, products, technologies, customers and logistics — so each should be managed separately.
points.quote: The said undertakings having distinct geographies, product profiles, technologies used, operational requirements, customer profile and base, market focus, logistics consideration, commercial considerations and growth opportunities.

points.point: The most concrete operating reason given is that the three mills run on three different pipe-making technologies, each needing its own specialised management and modernization programme — which maps exactly onto the three-way split.
points.quote: The manufacturing facilities operate on different technological platforms, including CPE technology at Nagothane, MPM technology at Mangaon and FQM technology at Telangana, each requiring specialized operational management, modernization initiatives and technical expertise.

points.point: Capital allocation is cited: pipes, drilling and renewables have different capital intensity, so separation is meant to let each assess and fund its own needs — relevant given the stalled INR852 crore capex plan and the INR350 crore Nagothane hot-mill upgrade never started.
points.quote: Efficient Capital Allocation: The manufacturing, drilling and renewable energy businesses have different capital intensity and funding requirements.

points.point: The rig is singled out for segregation on the grounds that it is commercially unlike pipe manufacturing — the same objection investors had raised on calls for two years.
points.quote: Focused Development of Rig Operations: The rig business has distinct operational and commercial characteristics as compared to the pipe manufacturing business.

points.point: The renewable plants are deliberately attached to the mills they sit beside rather than kept central, framed as energy-management efficiency and sustainability support for each business.
points.quote: The renewable power assets proposed to be transferred along with the respective undertakings are expected to provide better operational alignment, energy management efficiencies and support sustainability initiatives of the corresponding businesses.

points.point: Separate financial and operational reporting per entity is itself presented as a benefit — transparency and performance evaluation — which speaks to the calls where management refused to give product-wise or mill-wise margins.
points.quote: Improved Transparency and Value Creation: The proposed demerger would result in creation of focused business entities with independent financial and operational reporting, thereby enhancing transparency, improving performance evaluation and facilitating long-term value creation for stakeholders.

points.point: No cash is paid; shareholders receive 1 INR5 share in each resulting company per 5 MSL shares, giving identical proportionate ownership (promoter 70.3008%, public 29.6992%, 2,67,99,850 shares each) and, the board says, value neutrality.
points.quote: The above share exchange ratios shall ensure same proportionate shareholding structure of Resulting Company 1 and Resulting Company 2 with Demerged Company and hence Scheme shall be value neutral to the Demerged Company's shareholders.

points.point: Lenders are explicitly left untouched: no arrangement or compromise with creditors, liabilities travelling with each undertaking — i.e. the split is not presented as lender-driven or a debt restructuring.
points.quote: The liabilities towards the creditors of the Demerged Company and/or the Resulting Companies under the Scheme are neither being reduced nor being extinguished and the liabilities pertaining to the respective undertakings shall be assumed and discharged by the respective Resulting Companies in the ordinary course of business.

points.point: The plan was not stable: approved 22 May 2026, pulled back for review on 15 June 2026, and re-approved only on 7 October 2026 with tightened wording ('specified' rather than 'related' assets, 'same proportionate' rather than 'mirror' shareholding) and slightly revised indicative share counts (promoter 70.2784% to 70.3008%).
points.quote: This is further to the intimation dated 22nd May, 2026, about the approval of the Scheme of Arrangement by the Board of Directors of the Company, we have to inform you that the said Scheme is under further review and would be placed before any subsequent Board Meeting for its approval and would be submitted to Stock Exchanges thereafter.

points.point: The first hint of any separation was about the rig: asked whether MSL would keep two verticals, the Chairman declined to commit, while noting day rates had risen (~$40,000/day, expecting a new contract above $80,000).
points.quote: Well, we have to take the appropriate decision at the right time.

points.point: An investor asked outright about demerging or selling the rig business post-May 2025; management confirmed intent but no board discussion and no valuation expectation.
points.quote: It is something which we want to do, but it is subject to Board approval.

points.point: After an investor said the rig arrangement (MSL renting the rig to group company Jindal Drilling, which sub-contracts to ONGC) looked out of line with MSL's governance clean-up, management personally agreed and promised a communication once board approvals came.
points.quote: You are right, and I personally agree with you, but once suitable decisions and Board approvals are received, we will send communication on this.

points.point: Management confirmed a rig exit had been contemplated but that the board had given no update, while re-committing to pipes only — the rig had just been recontracted to Jindal Drilling at ~$35,000/day L1, with MSL to get ~$17,000-18,000/day.
points.quote: There was a view of getting out of the rig business, but we've not received any update from the Board in the Board meeting, which concluded yesterday.

points.point: A five-year shareholder explicitly demanded the company be split so investors could choose the pipe business over the treasury/holding activity, arguing the merged picture was unclear; management offered no response.
points.quote: Either divide the company in two parts. One should be a holding company, one should be a seamless company.

points.point: Six months before board approval, an analyst asked specifically about getting the Jindal Explorer rig off the books and was told there was no update, with the rig about to start a new ONGC contract.

points.point: On the last call before the first board approval, management described the future as cash conservation and opportunistic distressed acquisitions, with no mention of any restructuring, while defending the INR3,500 crore treasury against shareholders noting ~50% of market cap was cash.

points.point: The same call set out the economics of the Telangana asset that now forms United Seamless Limited: INR477 crores purchase plus INR73 crores reactivation, INR100-200 crores of EBITDA a year, and ~INR375 crores of tax saved from USTPL's INR1,500 crore-plus accumulated losses and unabsorbed depreciation.

No margin, cost, ROCE or valuation figures were given.

rationale.rationale: The separation at issue is the demerger of the Madura Fashion & Lifestyle (MFL) business — the four Lifestyle/Power brands (Louis Philippe, Van Heusen, Allen Solly, Peter England) plus the emerging portfolio of Reebok, American Eagle and Van Heusen Innerwear, and a contract-manufacturing/institutional arm — out of Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail Ltd (ABFRL, the Demerged Company) into Aditya Birla Lifestyle Brands Ltd (ABLBL, the Resulting Company), on a going-concern basis with 1:1 shares so holders own identical stakes in both; the Board approved it on April 19, 2024, NCLT sanctioned it on March 27, 2025, it became effective May 1, 2025, 1,22,02,94,773 shares were allotted May 26, 2025 (record date May 22, 2025) and ABLBL listed June 23, 2025. The reason management gave is capital allocation, stated most bluntly by Ashish Dikshit on the Feb 3, 2026 call: 'One of the primary reasons for demerger was to create an entity which can reinvest back more aggressively into growth' — because inside ABFRL the cash this branded business threw off 'was used to actually kick start or acquire multiple new businesses' (Aug 14, 2025), starving the mature brands of reinvestment. The quantification: the business generates roughly INR 900 crores of EBITDA cash, part to working capital and part to capex, where historical capex was 'close to 150 to 200 in the best years, maybe INR225 odd crores'; post-demerger FY26 capex went 'north of INR300 crores, perhaps INR320 crores, INR330 crores', funding 300+ gross store additions to 3,348 stores / 4.9 million sq ft across ~800 towns, 65 renovations in one quarter, and a new Pulivendula factory. Debt came across by formula — 'at the time of demerger, the company got the borrowings transferred based on the allocation formula' — about INR 800 crores at March 2025, peaking near INR 1,000 crores in September 2025 on festive inventory, INR 800 crores in December 2025 and INR 726 crores at March 2026 versus INR 781 crores a year earlier; INR 500 crores of NCDs repaid in January 2026 were refinanced with 'no fresh borrowing', and management guided to INR 200–300 crores of annual reduction and near-zero net debt in about three years, with capex ranked ahead of deleveraging ('Only the subsequent part will go towards debt reduction'). Management also kept repeating the structural promise that neither entity would raise equity except ABFRL's retained 'tomorrow' businesses, and demonstrated the self-funding claim with a maiden 50 paise dividend in year one and a stated 15–25%-of-PAT payout range. Growth is to be split by entity economics: Lifestyle Brands in early double digits on 6–7% (later '7%') steady-state LTL plus ~200 store adds a year, and the emerging brands at 18–20%+ (Dikshit: 'in excess of 20%'), rising to one-fourth of ABLBL in four to five years, with Reebok already doubled in sales and network tripled since acquisition and Van Heusen Innerwear losses halving on the way to break-even. Notably, no call or filing attributes the demerger request to any investor, lender or brand partner — it is presented purely as a board/strategy decision about where cash gets reinvested.
rationale.evolution: The Scheme itself dates to the April 19, 2024 board approval, with NCLT sanction on March 27, 2025 and effect from May 1, 2025, and the Aug 14, 2025 (Q1 FY26) call was the first as an independent listee — there Dikshit gave the rationale in answer to Niharika Karnani, that cash which had been used to kick-start or acquire new businesses inside ABFRL would now fund this business's own growth (capex first, debt reduction later, debt-free in 2.5–3 years, newer brands 18–20% vs Lifestyle early double digits). The Nov 5, 2025 (Q2 FY26) call barely revisited the rationale and instead exposed a transition cost: comparable prior-year segment numbers were missing because the business 'was part of the consolidated ABFRL', while net debt had risen ~INR 200 crores on festive and Bangladesh-related inventory build. On Feb 3, 2026 (Q3 FY26) the logic was restated most explicitly and tested — Ambit's Videesha Sheth challenged the INR 500 crore NCD board approval against the no-fundraise promise, management explained the demerger-allocated borrowings and pure refinancing, and Dikshit tied slower deleveraging directly to the demerger's purpose (capex INR 320–330 crores vs INR 150–225 crores historically), while guiding emerging brands to one-fourth of the company in 4–5 years. By May 8, 2026 (Q4 FY26) the narrative shifted from rationale to proof: 'a strong start to being an independent entity', 300+ stores added, net debt down to INR 726 crores, and the first dividend (50 paise) with a 15–25% payout framework, debt-free in three years but explicitly 'not something that we are chasing'.

rationale.rationale: Strictly read, Cello World is not spinning a business out to create value — it is collapsing a second listing, and the only 'separation' is a carve-out inside the group. The Composite Scheme of Arrangement (board-approved 12 Nov 2024) among Wim Plast Limited (WPL, the 55%-owned separately listed moulded-furniture/plastics maker — plastic moulded furniture, extrusion sheets, air coolers, dustbins, industrial pallets, industrial and engineering moulds, plus an investment book), Cello Consumer Products Private Limited (CCPPL, a wholly owned CWL subsidiary) and Cello World Limited does two things: WPL's Manufacturing Business (the 'Demerged Undertaking') is demerged and vested in CCPPL on a going-concern basis, and WPL's Remaining Business is amalgamated into CWL, after which WPL 'stands dissolved without winding up.' Management's stated reasons were blunt and structural, not margin-driven: Gaurav Rathod said on 13 Nov 2024 there were 'two rationales' — 'we do not see any point in running 2 separate listed entities as the business is not very different,' and WPL 'has a lot of manufacturing facilities… in different parts of the country wherein we can share manufacturing facilities with our other plastic product lines' — adding that it 'reduces our compliance while having it under Cello World,' and that since CWL already owned about 55% of WPL, 'it's only about 45% that is being acquired.' The scheme petition filed at NCLT lists three benefits: synergy of operations and economies of scale with 'the legal and regulatory compliances of both the listed entities… unified and streamlined'; 'consolidation of ownership interests in one listed company instead of two listed entities'; and a 'unified approach on customer engagement, distribution and supply chain management.' The numbers cited: a 0.86 aggregate swap (55 CWL shares of ₹5 per 100 WPL shares of ₹10 for the demerger plus 31 per 100 for the amalgamation), 46,53,239 new CWL shares (29,75,909 + 16,77,330), authorised capital reclassified to ₹140 crore / 28 crore shares, appointed date 1 April 2025, FY26 moulded furniture revenue ₹349 crore (−5% YoY; Q4 FY26 ₹91.5 crore, −13.5%) on ~39.5–40.9% gross margin with '62% of the cost of moulded furniture is actually polymer,' and the ₹100 crore WimPlast-to-CWL loan already repaid out of the ₹738 crore QIP. Pressure came from investors, not lenders or partners: Jay Doshi (14 Aug 2024) flagged merger enablement as a QIP objective, Aniket Kulkarni noted 'in the last couple of calls, I think we had spoken about the possibility of merging WimPlast,' Deepesh Sancheti asked the rationale twice, and Ashok Shah (13 Aug 2025) challenged whether the ratio was fair to WimPlast's 40–45% minority (CFO Atul Parolia: 'it will be beneficial to all'); the gating parties were SEBI/BSE/NSE (NOCs 2–3 July 2025), the shareholders and creditors (approved 6 Dec 2025, 201,355,406 shares for vs 17 against), and NCLT Ahmedabad (sanctioned 14 May 2026). Notably, management explicitly refused the opposite idea — when asked on 13 Nov 2024 whether the three verticals should be listed separately to enhance shareholder value, Rathod said no, 'otherwise, we would have not merged this back into Cello World,' because 'our furniture is very, very similar to our other plastic manufactured products.'
rationale.evolution: It surfaced first as an unresolved management wish on the 14 Aug 2024 call, framed as a QIP enabler and contingent on 'both the boards' — and the ₹100 crore WimPlast loan to CWL was repaid from QIP proceeds to clear the way. On the 13 Nov 2024 call the board had just approved the draft scheme and Rathod articulated the full two-part rationale (no point in two listed entities; shared plastic manufacturing capacity; lower compliance; only ~45% actually being acquired), while simultaneously rejecting an investor's suggestion to demerge the three verticals into separate listings. It then went quiet through the Feb 2025, May 2025 and Nov 2025 calls, resurfacing on 13 Aug 2025 when Parolia disclosed the 0.86 swap ratio already filed with the exchanges and Rathod said the needed SEBI permissions had come and 'now we are in the phase of merging'; on 16 Feb 2026 Parolia put the NCLT final hearing in the last week of February and completion within '2, 3 months' off the 1 April 2025 appointed date. By the 29 May 2026 call it was done — effective 27 May 2026, comparatives restated, and the forward-looking claim narrowed to 'the synergies between consumerware and moulded furniture can be explored further.'

points.point: Asked by Jay Doshi whether the QIP was partly to enable a WimPlast consolidation, Rathod confirmed management wanted the merger but had not yet obtained board decisions — it was still an intention, not a plan.
points.quote: In terms of WimPlast ideally, of course, from a management perspective we would like both of them to be merged and once it is decided by both the boards, I think we'll be able to go ahead on that as well.

points.point: With the board having just approved the draft scheme, Rathod gave the two core reasons: a second listed entity made no sense given overlapping businesses, and WimPlast's multi-location plants could be shared with Cello's other plastic lines.
points.quote: So, I think, we previously mentioned this as well, there are 2 rationales, one is that there is - we do not see any point in running 2 separate listed entities as the business is not very different.

points.point: Re-asked by Aniket Kulkarni, Rathod added compliance reduction and sized the transaction: CWL already held ~55% of WimPlast, so only the ~45% minority was being acquired, and WimPlast's spare manufacturing locations could serve other plastic product lines.
points.quote: Already because Cello World owns about 55% of the company in any case. So it's only about 45% that is being acquired.

points.point: Deepesh Sancheti proposed the reverse — demerging plastics, pens and glassware/consumerware into three separate listings — and Rathod rejected it outright as inconsistent with the WimPlast merger, citing manufacturing synergy between furniture and other moulded plastics.
points.quote: No, I think - I don't think we are looking at that because otherwise, we would have not merged this back into Cello World.

points.point: Pressed by Ashok Shah on whether the ratio disadvantaged WimPlast's minority holders versus Cello World's financials, Parolia disclosed the already-filed swap ratio of 0.86 and asserted the deal was beneficial to all; Rathod said the required SEBI permissions had come through.
points.quote: It's there already in the exchange. It's 0.86.

points.point: Rathod characterised the transaction as procedurally simple rather than structurally complex, with the only real hurdle being regulatory clearance, which had been received.
points.quote: It's not a complicated merger. It is just -- we needed some permissions from SEBI. And I think that's already come and now we are in the phase of merging.

points.point: Parolia gave the completion timeline — NCLT final hearing in the last week of February, roughly two to three months to close, with effect from the 1 April 2025 appointed date; Rathod confirmed Q1 FY27 completion.
points.quote: See, in the month of Feb only final hearing is there -- is around last week of Feb. And thereafter, once we get the approval, then everything is set, then we will be in the process of merging the thing.

points.point: Asked by Aniruddha whether all subsidiaries should likewise be merged for seamless capital flow and single billing, Rathod declined — the multi-subsidiary structure is deliberately kept to preserve unit-level P&L discipline, so the WimPlast merger was about removing a listing, not collapsing legal entities.
points.quote: So overall, while things can get easier, it also kind of dilutes the P&L of each and every unit and focus on unit economics kind of goes away.

points.point: Rathod confirmed completion and stated the only forward-looking benefit in explicit terms — exploring synergies between consumerware and moulded furniture — in the same quarter moulded furniture revenue fell 13.5% YoY to ₹91.5 crore.
points.quote: We have completed the merger of Wimplast Limited with Cello World. With this integration, the synergies between consumerware and moulded furniture can be explored further.

points.point: Parolia closed the loop on accounting: the scheme became effective 27 May 2026 with a 1 April 2025 appointed date, forcing restatement of comparatives and a consequential EPS impact for shares pending issuance.
points.quote: Lastly, I would like to inform that composite scheme of arrangement among Wimplast, Cello Consumer Products Limited and the company has become effective from 27th May 2026, with an appointed date of 1st April 2025 as defined under the scheme.

points.point: The scheme's two legs: WimPlast's Manufacturing Business (the Demerged Undertaking) is demerged into CCPPL, a wholly owned CWL subsidiary, on a going-concern basis, with CWL — not CCPPL — issuing the consideration shares to WimPlast's non-CWL shareholders.

points.point: The second leg extinguishes WimPlast entirely — its residual business folds into CWL and the company is dissolved without winding up, ending the dual listing; the 6 Dec 2025 vote was 201,355,406 shares for versus 17 against.

rationale.what_management_expects: For Cello World: one listed entity, unified and streamlined compliance for both, consolidated ownership, economies of scale, shared multi-location plastic manufacturing, a unified customer/distribution/supply-chain approach, and newly explorable consumerware–moulded-furniture synergies. For the furniture business inside CCPPL: no revenue re-rating — low single-digit growth, EBIT lifted only by premiumisation and outdoor furniture. No margin, capital-release or valuation target was quantified.
rationale.gaps: No quantified synergies, cost savings or EPS accretion; no reason manufacturing went to CCPPL rather than CWL; no valuation basis for 55:31; no tax or minority-exit detail.

rationale.rationale: The business being separated is not a pharma business at all: it is the Life Sciences business and the Digital Innovation business of Arco Lab Private Limited, Strides' wholly owned Global Capability Centre (GCC), carved out into a new wholly owned subsidiary, Pivot Path Private Limited, under a Sections 230–232 Scheme of Arrangement, and then majority-sold. Management's stated reason is that this unit — built inside Arco Lab across life sciences consulting, digital transformation, quality and compliance, and technology-enabled operational services — outgrew its captive role: 'As demand from external pharmaceutical and life sciences companies grew, the business evolved into an independent platform serving industry-leading customers.' The filings name four problems the separation solves: supporting its next phase of growth, serving global customers effectively, building agentic-AI platforms, and enabling access to external capital — none of which a cost-centre inside a pharma manufacturer can fund or staff. The numbers cited are modest and explain why it is not core to Strides: FY26 revenue of ₹1,447 million (including revenues for services rendered to Strides) — just 3% of Strides' turnover — with EBITDA of ₹169 million, net worth of ₹100 million standalone (0.3% of Strides' net worth) and ₹360 million consolidated (1%). Ascent Capital (through Ascent Growth Trust) with co-investor Vintage Classic Limited values Pivot Path at ~₹2,300 million post-money; Strides realises ~₹1,000 million (₹750 million at closing, ₹250 million on the first anniversary), keeps 19.95%, and Ascent injects ₹500 million of primary capital, leaving Investors 65.05% and a 15% ESOP pool, with Pivot Path reclassified as an Associate. Badree Komandur frames it as Strides' repeatable playbook — 'Strides' proven capability to identify, incubate and scale high-potential businesses' — that 'unlocks value for Strides, provides Pivot Path with the resources to scale independently, and allows Strides to retain meaningful participation in its future success,' while also 'strengthens the Company's balance sheet.' No investor, lender or partner is named as having demanded the separation; the pull came from external life-sciences customers and from the incoming financial investor, whose rationale (per Raja Kumar) is to pair 400+ subject matter experts with technology and agentic AI in 'core, non-discretionary segments of the pharmaceutical industry.' Pricing rests on an independent valuation by a SEBI-registered merchant banker, and the deal is declared not a related party transaction and outside Regulation 37A.
rationale.evolution: The idea does not appear in a single one of the thirteen earnings calls; it exists only in the filings, which reference an intimation of May 15, 2025 for the Arco Lab–Pivot Path scheme, with an Appointed Date of April 10, 2025 — i.e. the carve-out was in motion for more than a year unmentioned. NCLT Bengaluru pronounced approval on May 18, 2026 (the same day as the Q4 FY26 board meeting whose call, on May 18, 2026, discussed only US/ex-US growth, margins and deleveraging), the order hit the NCLT portal May 20, 2026, the certified copy arrived May 25, 2026, and the Scheme became effective June 1, 2026. Only on June 27, 2026 did the plan's second leg surface: the board approved selling a majority stake to the Ascent Capital consortium, converting what the Scheme had set up as a wholly owned subsidiary into a ~20%-held Associate. The nearest the calls come is context on the earlier OneSource/softgel playbook — Arco Lab named as the wholly owned subsidiary parking the OneSource stake (May 22, 2025 call) and the ₹78.8 billion returned to shareholders via that demerger and listing (July 29, 2025 call).

points.point: The separated business is Arco Lab's Life Sciences business plus its Digital Innovation business, demerged into Pivot Path under Sections 230–232, with Appointed Date April 10, 2025 and NCLT approval pronounced May 18, 2026.
points.quote: The Scheme provides for the demerger of Arco Lab’s Life Sciences business and Digital Innovation business (the “Demerged Undertaking”) into Pivot Path, pursuant to Sections 230–232 of the Companies Act, 2013 and other applicable provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder (“Scheme”).

points.point: The stated purpose of the carve-out is growth capacity, global customer service, agentic-AI platform building and access to outside capital — things it could not do as a captive GCC unit.
points.quote: To support its next phase of growth, serve global customers effectively, build agentic-AI platforms, and enable access to external capital, the business was carved out into Pivot Path pursuant to a Scheme of Arrangement approved by the Hon'ble National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) in May 2026.

points.point: The trigger was external demand: a unit originally serving Strides internally began winning third-party pharma and life-sciences customers and became a standalone platform.
points.quote: As demand from external pharmaceutical and life sciences companies grew, the business evolved into an independent platform serving industry-leading customers.

points.point: Strides positions it as a repeatable incubate-and-unlock model rather than a disposal of a problem asset, keeping economic participation.
points.quote: The transaction reflects Strides' strategy of creating, scaling and unlocking value from high-potential businesses while retaining participation in their future growth.

points.point: Scale cited: FY26 revenue ₹1,447 million (3% of Strides' turnover) and EBITDA ₹169 million; net worth ₹100 million standalone (0.3%) and ₹360 million consolidated (1%) — small enough that it is clearly non-core.
points.quote: For FY26, the carved-out business reported revenue of ₹1,447 million (including revenues for services rendered to Strides) and EBITDA of ₹169 million, demonstrating its operating scale and growth trajectory.

points.point: Economics: ~₹2,300m post-money valuation, ~₹1,000m realised by Strides (₹750m at closing, ₹250m after one year), ₹500m primary infusion by Ascent, Strides left at 19.95% with Investors 65.05% and a 15% ESOP pool.
points.quote: The transaction values Pivot Path at ~₹2,300m on a post-money basis, enables Strides to realise ~₹1,000m while retaining a ~20% stake, and includes a primary capital infusion of ₹500 million to accelerate Pivot Path's next phase of growth.

points.point: Badree Komandur's framing of the three-way benefit — cash and balance-sheet strength for Strides, independent scaling resources for Pivot Path, retained upside.
points.quote: This transaction unlocks value for Strides, provides Pivot Path with the resources to scale independently, and allows Strides to retain meaningful participation in its future success.

points.point: Accounting consequence: Pivot Path drops out of consolidation and becomes an Associate; the deal is declared non-related-party, priced off an independent SEBI-registered merchant banker valuation.
points.quote: Upon completion of the transaction, Pivot Path shall be reclassified as an Associate Company.

points.point: The incoming investor's rationale: 400+ subject matter experts applying technology and agentic AI to compliance, digital transformation and drug safety in non-discretionary pharma spend.
points.quote: Pivot Path brings deep domain expertise across the core, non-discretionary segments of the pharmaceutical industry, capabilities that have been rigorously honed within the Strides stable.

points.point: The Q4 FY26 call, held May 18, 2026 — the very day NCLT pronounced the Pivot Path order — never mentions Pivot Path, Arco Lab or any carve-out; the three-year strategy is described purely in pharma terms.
points.quote: Over the last 3 years, we have been very clear on our priorities, geographical diversification, profitability and balance sheet strength.

points.point: The only call-level support for the value-unlocking logic is the OneSource precedent, cited as the company's demonstrated way of returning value to shareholders.
points.quote: And the recent one being we distributed INR 78.8 billion back to shareholders in the form of demerger and listing.

points.point: Arco Lab — the entity Pivot Path was later carved out of — is discussed on the calls only as the wholly owned subsidiary holding the residual 1.6% OneSource stake, with no hint of a services business inside it.
points.quote: So we retained this in Arco Lab, which is a wholly owned subsidiary of Strides.

rationale.what_management_expects: For Pivot Path: ₹500m primary capital, resources to scale independently, serve global customers, build agentic-AI platforms, access external capital and Ascent's expertise, plus a 15% ESOP pool. For Strides: ~₹1,000m realised (₹750m at closing, ₹250m at one year), a strengthened balance sheet, and a ~20% associate stake retaining upside. No margin, focus or re-rating claims are made.
rationale.gaps: Calls never mention Pivot Path or Arco Lab's demerger. No use of proceeds, no reason for selling majority rather than listing, no customer, employee or related-party-pricing detail.

judge.what_is_spun: The Power Transmission Business: high-speed and niche low-speed gearboxes, defence products, aftermarket and retro-fitment services
judge.reason: Management states the demerger of the Power Transmission business is "to unlock value and to drive operational efficiencies", alongside amalgamation of Sir Shadi Lal Enterprises, leading to independent listing of TPTL.
judge.insiders: Tarun Sawhney (promoter) appointed TPTL Vice Chairman & Managing Director for five years; Dhruv M. Sawhney non-executive Chairman; Nikhil Sawhney director. 3.13 crore shares locked in to Oct 2027/2029; stake % not stated.
judge.hidden_value: A ~35-36% PBIT-margin global gearbox and defence business buried inside a sugar company: only 4.45% of turnover yet 13.40% of cost-of-acquisition allocation, order book just under ₹500 crore (up 25%), ₹340 crore capex enabling about ₹700 crore output.
judge.selling_pressure_why: Small spin (13.4% of cost allocation), 1-for-3 entitlement, engineering/defence shares handed to sugar-commodity holders; 7.35 crore of 10.48 crore shares free.
judge.listing_timeline: Per TPTL letter dated October 9, 2026: "the equity shares of the Company shall be listed and admitted to dealings on BSE and NSE with effect from October 12, 2026" (BSE 544824, NSE TRIVENIPT, 10,47,54,338 shares of Re.2/- each); earlier, on the June 4, 2026 call management said "by the end of August, we will have a listing of Triveni Power Transmissions Limited."
judge.read_next: TPTL's first standalone quarterly results and order book after the ₹340 crore capex completes in September 2026.
judge.quote: As power transmission migrates into Triveni Power Transmission Limited, the company is armed with sufficient cash flows and a balance sheet to be able to incur all of this CapEx and OpEx and more.
